claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by simultaneous, rapid reduction and nucleation of all constituent metal ions.
Well-matched precursor-reduction rates combined with a rapid temperature ramp cause all constituent elements to nucleate concurrently.
Concurrent nucleation kinetically traps a homogeneous, single-phase alloy before substantial elemental segregation or phase separation occurs.
A steep thermal spike will produce more homogeneous nanoparticles than a conventional slower heating protocol reaching the same peak temperature.
The rapid protocol consists of heating above approximately 700 °C within seconds followed by rapid quenching.
The baseline protocol uses a minutes-long ramp to the same peak temperature as the rapid protocol.
The controlled comparison holds atmosphere, composition, precursor concentration, support, and peak temperature constant while changing the heating protocol.
Rapidly heated nanoparticles will form a homogeneous alloy phase without detectable phase-separated domains.
Rapid thermal input forces the metal precursors to reduce nearly concurrently.
Nearly concurrent reduction promotes synchronous nucleation.
Kinetic trapping in a metastable mixed state overcomes precursor-specific reduction-kinetic differences that would otherwise permit diffusion-limited phase separation.
Rapid heating will yield a higher degree of phase and elemental homogeneity than slow heating.
Slow heating permits sequential reduction of individual metals and consequently produces elemental segregation or phase-separated domains.
The proposed mechanism applies when constituent noble-metal precursors have sufficiently similar reduction behavior for synchronized nucleation to be feasible.
The mechanism may not apply when ligands or supports substantially alter reduction kinetics or when the constituents have highly disparate redox properties.
Comparative studies of synthesis routes support kinetic trapping through rapid heating.
Differences in precursor chemistry make exact phase homogeneity uncertain across high-entropy compositions.
A lack of statistically significant improvement in phase homogeneity under rapid heating relative to slow heating would falsify the hypothesis.
